Teen Smartphone Usage and Addiction Impact Dataset

Aleksandra Dobosz, Aleksandra Engel, Adam Gonet, Kamil Laskowski

2026-05-04

Teen Smartphone Usage and Addiction Impact Dataset

About the Project

This is an R version of project conducted for Machine Learning project in Python. All codes are fully converted into R version, comments and descriptions for preparation and modelling parts are taken from the python version of this project.

This version is additionally extended by adding additional data and prediction on this new set of data. This is the last part of this report. The goal is to check and experiment how ML modelling is different in R and if the model can achieve satisfactory results on randomly generated data.

About the Dataset

This dataset, sourced from Kaggle, focuses on understanding smartphone usage patterns among teenagers and the impact of excessive phone use on their academic performance, mental health, and daily lifestyle. With the rapid increase in smartphone dependency among adolescents, it has become important to study how usage habits influence well-being and performance.

The dataset captures multiple aspects of teenage behavior, including addiction levels, time distribution across activities, sleep patterns, social interactions, and mental health indicators. From our perspective, we aim to build regression models to examine which factors have the greatest impact on smartphone addiction levels.

Column Descriptions

Demographic Information

  • ID: Unique identifier for each student
  • Name: Name of the student
  • Age: Age of the teenager
  • Gender: Gender of the student
  • Location: Geographic location
  • School_Grade: Current academic or level

Smartphone Usage & Time Distribution

  • Daily_Usage_Hours: Average smartphone usage per day (hours)
  • Weekend_Usage_Hours: Average smartphone usage on weekends
  • Screen_Time_Before_Bed: Screen time before going to sleep
  • Phone_Checks_Per_Day: Number of times the phone is checked daily
  • Apps_Used_Daily: Number of apps used per day

Activity-Based Usage

  • Time_on_Social_Media: Hours spent on social media platforms
  • Time_on_Gaming: Hours spent on mobile gaming
  • Time_on_Education: Hours spent on educational activities
  • Phone_Usage_Purpose: Primary purpose of smartphone usage

Health & Lifestyle Indicators

  • Sleep_Hours: Average hours of sleep per day
  • Exercise_Hours: Time spent on physical exercise
  • Anxiety_Level: Indicator of anxiety level
  • Depression_Level: Indicator of depression level
  • Self_Esteem: Self-esteem score

Social & Family Factors

  • Social_Interactions: Level of in-person social interaction
  • Family_Communication: Quality or frequency of communication with family
  • Parental_Control: Level of parental monitoring or restrictions

Outcome Variables

  • Academic_Performance: Indicator of academic performance
  • Addiction_Level: Level of smartphone addiction (target variable)

Problem Description

Smartphone use has become an essential part of teenagers’ daily lives, but excessive usage may lead to addiction and negatively affect mental health, sleep patterns, social interactions, and academic performance. Smartphone addiction among adolescents is an increasingly important social and psychological issue. The goal of this project is to use regression analysis to identify which behavioral, lifestyle, and psychological factors most strongly influence the level of smartphone addiction. Understanding these relationships can support early intervention and promote healthier smartphone usage habits among teenagers.

Section 2: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing

Now we’ll remove unnecessary columns and split the data into training and test sets. Then, we’ll apply one-hot encoding to categorical variables.

Step 1: Remove non-informative columns

Columns like ‘Name’ and ‘ID’ don’t contribute to predictions since they are just identifiers. We’ll drop them to reduce noise.

# remove selected columns using dplyr
df <- df %>% select(-Name, -ID)

Step 2: Train-Test Split

We split the data into 80% training and 20% testing sets. Using random_state=123, which ensures reproducibility.

set.seed(123)

index <- createDataPartition(df[[1]], p = 0.8, list = FALSE)

df_train <- df[index, ]
df_test  <- df[-index, ]

Section 3: Exploratory Data Analysis

This section analyzes relationships between variables, target variable distribution, and statistical significance tests.

#only numeric columns
numeric_df <- df_train[sapply(df_train, is.numeric)]

#calculate Kendall correlation matrix, because it's robust to non-normal distributions
corr <- cor(numeric_df, method = "kendall", use = "complete.obs")

  • < 0.2 – no linear correlation
  • 0.2 – 0.4 – low linear correlation
  • 0.4 -0.7 – mid linear correlation
  • 0.7 – 0.9 – strong linear correlation
  • > 0.9 – very strong linear correlation

Correlation analysis shows that addiction level is most strongly associated with usage-intensity features, especially Daily_Usage_Hours, as well as Apps_Used_Daily, Time_on_Social_Media, Phone_Checks_Per_Day and Time_on_Gaming. A negative correlation with Sleep_Hours suggests that higher addiction levels are linked to reduced sleep, while most other variables show only weak relationships.

# skewness of target variable
skewness(df_train$Addiction_Level, na.rm = TRUE)
## [1] -1.589696

Let’s try log and square root transformations to improve normality

# Histogram - original data
p1 <- ggplot(df_train, aes(x = Addiction_Level)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#21918c", color = "#21918c") +
  labs(title = "Histogram - Addiction_Level") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Histogram - log transformed
p2 <- ggplot(df_train, aes(x = log(Addiction_Level))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#21918c", color = "#21918c") +
  labs(title = "Histogram - log(Addiction_Level)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Arrange plots side by side
grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)

Log scaling doesn’t improve the distribution of target variable - let’s try square root.

# Histogram - original data
p1 <- ggplot(df_train, aes(x = Addiction_Level)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#21918c", color = "#21918c") +
  labs(title = "Histogram - Addiction_Level") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Histogram - sqrt transformed data
p2 <- ggplot(df_train, aes(x = sqrt(Addiction_Level))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#21918c", color = "#21918c") +
  labs(title = "Histogram - sqrt(Addiction_Level)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Arrange plots side by side
grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)

# Original data
skew_original <- skewness(df_train$Addiction_Level, na.rm = TRUE)
kurt_original <- kurtosis(df_train$Addiction_Level, na.rm = TRUE)

# Square root transformation
skew_sqrt <- skewness(sqrt(df_train$Addiction_Level), na.rm = TRUE)
kurt_sqrt <- kurtosis(sqrt(df_train$Addiction_Level), na.rm = TRUE)

# Log transformation
skew_log <- skewness(log(df_train$Addiction_Level), na.rm = TRUE)
kurt_log <- kurtosis(log(df_train$Addiction_Level), na.rm = TRUE)

# Print results
cat("Original:")
## Original:
cat(" Skewness:", skew_original)
##  Skewness: -1.589696
cat(" Kurtosis:", kurt_original)
##  Kurtosis: 2.10591
cat("Sqrt transformed:")
## Sqrt transformed:
cat(" Skewness:", skew_sqrt)
##  Skewness: -1.985016
cat(" Kurtosis:", kurt_sqrt)
##  Kurtosis: 4.601342
cat("Log transformed:")
## Log transformed:
cat(" Skewness:", skew_log)
##  Skewness: -2.70758
cat(" Kurtosis:", kurt_log)
##  Kurtosis: 11.03116

The target variable Addiction_Level will be modeled in its original scale. Applied transformations such as square root and logarithm increased skewness and kurtosis and even less normal distribution. Since most machine learning models do not require the target variable to follow a normal distribution, keeping the original form is the most appropriate choice.

Statistical Analysis

# Violin plot: distribution by school grade
ggplot(df_train, aes(x = School_Grade, y = Addiction_Level)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "#7ad151", color = "#7ad151") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, outlier.size = 1, alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Addiction_Level by school grade") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))

# Perform Kruskal-Wallis test
kruskal_result <- kruskal.test(Addiction_Level ~ School_Grade, data = df_train)

# Print p-value
cat(sprintf("Kruskal-Wallis p-value = %.5f\n", kruskal_result$p.value))
## Kruskal-Wallis p-value = 0.88581

To statistically verify the visual differences observed in the violin plot, we applied Kruskal–Wallis. This non-parametric test was chosen due to the non-normal distribution of the target variable and the presence of multiple groups. The results indicate that there is no significant difference between addiction level across school grades.

Section 4: Feature Engineering

We’ll create derived features to capture behavioral patterns, reduce dimensionality, and improve model performance.

One-hot-encoding on Gender, School_Grade & Phone_Usage_Purpose

df_train_encoded <- model.matrix(~ Gender + School_Grade + Phone_Usage_Purpose, data = df_train) |> as.data.frame()

df_train_encoded <- df_train_encoded[, !names(df_train_encoded) %in% "(Intercept)"]

# Keeping only encoded
df_train <- cbind(df_train[, !names(df_train) %in% c("Gender", "School_Grade", "Phone_Usage_Purpose")],
            df_train_encoded)

Additional features

We created additional features to better capture behavioral patterns related to smartphone usage, including usage intensity, night-time activity, and lifestyle balance.

  • Total_Phone_Time – total daily time spent on the phone, calculated as the sum of social media, gaming, and educational usage. It represents overall smartphone exposure.
  • Checks_per_Hour – the number of phone checks normalized by daily usage hours, capturing compulsive checking behavior rather than long continuous sessions.
  • Night_Usage_Ratio – the proportion of total phone usage that occurs before bedtime, reflecting potentially unhealthy night-time usage patterns.
  • Digital_Life_Balance – a ratio combining sleep and physical activity relative to phone usage, indicating the balance between offline lifestyle and digital behavior.
  • Entertainment_to_Education_Ratio – the relationship between entertainment-related phone use (social media and gaming) and educational use, distinguishing productive from leisure-oriented behavior.
  • Exercise_Level – a categorical variable derived from weekly exercise hours, grouping physical activity into very low, low, moderate, and high levels to improve interpretability.
df_train$Total_Phone_Time <- df_train$Time_on_Social_Media + df_train$Time_on_Gaming + df_train$Time_on_Education
df_train$Checks_per_Hour <- df_train$Phone_Checks_Per_Day / (df_train$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)
df_train$Night_Usage_Ratio <- df_train$Screen_Time_Before_Bed / (df_train$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)
df_train$Digital_Life_Balance <- (df_train$Exercise_Hours + df_train$Sleep_Hours) / (df_train$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)

df_train$Entertainment_to_Education_Ratio <-(df_train$Time_on_Social_Media + df_train$Time_on_Gaming) / (df_train$Time_on_Education + 1e-12)

df_train$Exercise_Level <- cut(df_train$Exercise_Hours, breaks = c(-1, 1, 3, 6, 20), labels = c("Very Low", "Low", "Moderate", "High"))
exercise_dummies <- model.matrix(~ Exercise_Level, data = df_train) |>as.data.frame()
exercise_dummies <- exercise_dummies[, !names(exercise_dummies) %in% "(Intercept)"]
df_train <- cbind(df_train[, !names(df_train) %in% "Exercise_Level"], exercise_dummies)

At this step for python version from Machine Learning 1 course we’ve taken code for downcasting our dataframe. The function downcast_dataframe() is used to reduce the memory usage of a DataFrame by converting each column to the smallest possible data type that can still hold all its values. Downcasting can reduce memory usage by 50–90%.

In R version we decided to omit this function - R primarily operates with just two numeric types (integer and double), and more granular downcasting is not easily supported and would require additional packages. Taking into consideration our small dataset and very little potential memory savings the change would be neglible.

# Apply same transformations to test set

# Drop location
df_test <- df_test[, !names(df_test) %in% "Location"]

# One-hot
test_dummies <- model.matrix(~ Gender + School_Grade + Phone_Usage_Purpose, data = df_test) |> as.data.frame()
test_dummies <- test_dummies[, !names(test_dummies) %in% "(Intercept)"]
df_test <- cbind(df_test[, !names(df_test) %in% c("Gender", "School_Grade", "Phone_Usage_Purpose")], test_dummies)

# New features
df_test$Total_Phone_Time <- df_test$Time_on_Social_Media + df_test$Time_on_Gaming + df_test$Time_on_Education
df_test$Checks_per_Hour <- df_test$Phone_Checks_Per_Day / (df_test$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)
df_test$Night_Usage_Ratio <- df_test$Screen_Time_Before_Bed / (df_test$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)
df_test$Digital_Life_Balance <- (df_test$Exercise_Hours + df_test$Sleep_Hours) / (df_test$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)

df_test$Entertainment_to_Education_Ratio <- (df_test$Time_on_Social_Media + df_test$Time_on_Gaming) /     (df_test$Time_on_Education + 1e-3)

df_test$Exercise_Level <- cut( df_test$Exercise_Hours, breaks = c(-1, 1, 3, 6, 20), labels = c("Very Low", "Low", "Moderate", "High"))
exercise_dummies_test <- model.matrix(~ Exercise_Level, data = df_test) |> as.data.frame()
exercise_dummies_test <- exercise_dummies_test[, !names(exercise_dummies_test) %in% "(Intercept)"]
df_test <- cbind(df_test[, !names(df_test) %in% "Exercise_Level"], exercise_dummies_test)
setdiff(names(df_train), names(df_test))
## character(0)
setdiff(names(df_test), names(df_train))
## character(0)

Section 5: Model Training with Decision Tree Regressor

We’ll build a Decision Tree Regressor with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and 5-fold cross-validation.

Reason for choosing this model for our problem:

Baseline model - Trees are interpretable and capture non-linear relationships without requiring feature scaling Feature importance - Directly reveals which variables matter most for predicting addiction No assumptions - Unlike linear models, doesn’t assume linear relationships between predictors and addiction level

Step 1: Prepare training and test data

# Separate predictors and target variable

x_train <- df_train %>%
  select(-Addiction_Level)

y_train <- df_train$Addiction_Level

x_test <- df_test %>%
  select(-Addiction_Level)

y_test <- df_test$Addiction_Level
set.seed(42)

cv_control <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 5
)
# create copies for modeling
df_train_model <- df_train
df_test_model <- df_test

# remove target before NZV check
predictors_train <- df_train_model %>%
  select(-Addiction_Level)

predictors_test <- df_test_model %>%
  select(-Addiction_Level)

# detect near-zero variance predictors
nzv <- nearZeroVar(predictors_train)

# remove problematic predictors
if(length(nzv) > 0){
  predictors_train <- predictors_train[, -nzv]
  predictors_test <- predictors_test[, -nzv]
}

# add target back
df_train_model <- cbind(
  Addiction_Level = df_train_model$Addiction_Level,
  predictors_train
)

df_test_model <- cbind(
  Addiction_Level = df_test_model$Addiction_Level,
  predictors_test
)

cat("Removed predictors:", length(nzv), "\n")
## Removed predictors: 2
# sanity check
"Addiction_Level" %in% names(df_train_model)
## [1] TRUE
set.seed(42)

dt_model <- rpart(
  Addiction_Level ~ .,
  data = df_train_model,
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(
    minsplit = 2,
    minbucket = 5,
    cp = 0,
    maxdepth = 30
  )
)



rpart.plot(dt_model, 
           type = 2,
           extra = 101,
           fallen.leaves = TRUE,
           box.palette = viridis(100, option = "D")
           )

# Predictions
dt_predictions <- predict(
  dt_model,
  newdata = df_test_model
)

# Metrics
dt_results <- postResample(
  pred = dt_predictions,
  obs = df_test_model$Addiction_Level
)

print(dt_results)
##      RMSE  Rsquared       MAE 
## 0.8962308 0.6957902 0.5394673

The R implementation achieved performance metrics comparable to the original Python model. Although slight differences were observed (likely due to implementation differences between DecisionTreeRegressor in scikit-learn and rpart in R), the overall predictive performance remained similar, confirming successful model reproduction. The Decision Tree achieved strong predictive performance with an R² of 0.696, meaning it explains 69.6% of the variance in addiction levels. On average, predictions deviate by 0.539 points (MAE) from actual addiction scores.

Section 6: Model Training with Random Forest Regressor

Random Forest builds multiple decision trees and averages predictions for better generalization.

Reason for choosing this model for our problem: - Reduces overfitting - Multiple trees with bootstrapped samples and feature randomness create robust predictions - Feature importance ranking - Aggregates importance across all trees, giving reliable feature rankings - Robust to outliers - our target variable distribution has skewness and outliers and Random Forest is less sensitive for them

set.seed(42)

names(df_train_model)[
  names(df_train_model) == "Phone_Usage_PurposeSocial Media"
] <- "Phone_Usage_PurposeSocialMedia"

names(df_test_model)[
  names(df_test_model) == "Phone_Usage_PurposeSocial Media"] <- "Phone_Usage_PurposeSocialMedia"
# Train Random Forest Regressor
rf_model <- randomForest(
  Addiction_Level ~ .,
  data = df_train_model,
  ntree = 400,         # n_estimators
  mtry = floor(ncol(df_train_model[-1]) * 0.5),  # max_features = 0.5
  nodesize = 1,        # min_samples_leaf = 1
  importance = TRUE
)

print(rf_model)
## 
## Call:
##  randomForest(formula = Addiction_Level ~ ., data = df_train_model,      ntree = 400, mtry = floor(ncol(df_train_model[-1]) * 0.5),      nodesize = 1, importance = TRUE) 
##                Type of random forest: regression
##                      Number of trees: 400
## No. of variables tried at each split: 17
## 
##           Mean of squared residuals: 0.2774051
##                     % Var explained: 89.48
# Predictions
rf_predictions <- predict(
  rf_model,
  newdata = df_test_model
)

# Metrics
rf_results <- postResample(
  pred = rf_predictions,
  obs = df_test_model$Addiction_Level
)

print(rf_results)
##      RMSE  Rsquared       MAE 
## 0.5270994 0.9016737 0.3713318

This Random Forest model was successfully reproduced in R, achieving nearly identical predictive performance to the original Python implementation. Minor metric differences are expected due to implementation differences between scikit-learn and randomForest in R.

The Random Forest model significantly outperforms the Decision Tree, achieving an R² of 0.9016 (explaining 90.16% of variance in addiction levels) with a lower MAE of 0.371, demonstrating that ensemble methods with multiple trees and bootstrap sampling effectively reduce overfitting and capture complex behavioral patterns in smartphone addiction prediction.

Section 7: Model Training with AdaBoost Regressor

AdaBoost builds an ensemble of weak learners, focusing on instances that previous models found difficult.

Reason for choosing this model for our problem: - Sequential learning - Focuses on instances the previous model misclassified, reducing bias and variance - Handles difficult cases - Emphasizes harder-to-predict addiction levels, improving overall performance - Adaptive weighting - Learns which samples are most informative for addiction prediction task - Prevents underfitting - Particularly useful when simpler models underfit complex behavioral patterns

set.seed(42)

# Train boosting model

ada_model <- gbm(
  formula = Addiction_Level ~ .,
  data = df_train_model,
  distribution = "gaussian",
  n.trees = 100,          # n_estimators
  interaction.depth = 2, # max_depth = 2
  shrinkage = 0.05,      # learning_rate
  bag.fraction = 1.0,
  cv.folds = 5,
  verbose = FALSE
)

# Debbuged with ChatGPT to match viridis

imp <- summary(ada_model, plotit = FALSE)

ggplot(imp,
       aes(
         x = reorder(var, rel.inf),
         y = rel.inf)) +
  geom_col(fill = viridis(1)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Relative Influence"
    ) + theme_minimal()

# Predictions
ada_predictions <- predict(
  ada_model,
  newdata = df_test_model,
  n.trees = 100
)

# Metrics
ada_results <- postResample(
  pred = ada_predictions,
  obs = df_test_model$Addiction_Level
)

print(ada_results)
##      RMSE  Rsquared       MAE 
## 0.7389755 0.8036426 0.5405943

Due to implementation limitations of AdaBoost regression in R, a gradient boosting approach (gbm) was used as the closest available alternative. The reproduced model achieved improved predictive performance compared to the original Python implementation.

The boosting model in R achieved better predictive performance than the original Python implementation (RMSE = 0.739 vs. 1.003; R² = 0.804 vs. 0.564). This difference is likely explained by implementation differences, as the Python model relied on AdaBoostRegressor, whereas the R version used gradient boosting (gbm), which is generally more flexible and capable of capturing complex relationships in the data.

Section 8: Predictions on added set of new data

Lastly in our project we wanted to check whether predictions on the generated data will be as good as on the original dataset. In our R pipline Random Forest was the best predictive performance, obtaining the lowest RMSE (0.527) and MAE (0.371). To check that we created the python scripts, which generates 500 new lines of observations each time.

This part was partially coded with the ChatGPT due to ensure reprudicibility on different enviroment not only on those used byt the authors.

# run script - requirements with fallbacks
python_cmd <- Sys.which("python3")
conda_python <- "/opt/anaconda3/bin/python"

if (file.exists(conda_python)) {python_cmd <- conda_python}
if (python_cmd == "") {stop("Python not found.")}

script_path <- "../scripts/generate_new_records.py"

if (!file.exists(script_path)) {stop("Script not found. Check your working directory with getwd().")}

old_wd <- getwd()
on.exit(setwd(old_wd))

setwd("..")

system2(python_cmd, "scripts/generate_new_records.py")
new_records <- read.csv("../scripts/new_records.csv")

# Cleaning 
new_records_predictors <- new_records[, !names(new_records) %in% "Addiction_Level"]
new_records_predictors <- new_records_predictors %>% select(-Name, -ID, -Location)

# One-hot encoding like in training/test
new_records_encoded <- model.matrix(~ Gender + School_Grade + Phone_Usage_Purpose, data = new_records_predictors) |> as.data.frame()
new_records_encoded <- new_records_encoded[ , !names(new_records_encoded) %in% "(Intercept)"]
new_records_model <- cbind(new_records_predictors[ , !names(new_records_predictors) %in% c("Gender", "School_Grade", "Phone_Usage_Purpose")], new_records_encoded)

# Same new features
new_records_model$Total_Phone_Time <- new_records_model$Time_on_Social_Media + new_records_model$Time_on_Gaming + new_records_model$Time_on_Education
new_records_model$Checks_per_Hour <- new_records_model$Phone_Checks_Per_Day / (new_records_model$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)
new_records_model$Night_Usage_Ratio <- new_records_model$Screen_Time_Before_Bed / (new_records_model$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)
new_records_model$Digital_Life_Balance <- (new_records_model$Exercise_Hours + new_records_model$Sleep_Hours) / (new_records_model$Daily_Usage_Hours + 1e-12)
new_records_model$Entertainment_to_Education_Ratio <- (new_records_model$Time_on_Social_Media + new_records_model$Time_on_Gaming) /(new_records_model$Time_on_Education + 1e-12)
new_records_model$Exercise_Level <- cut(new_records_model$Exercise_Hours, breaks = c(-1, 1, 3, 6, 20), labels = c("Very Low", "Low", "Moderate", "High"))

exercise_dummies_new <- model.matrix(~ Exercise_Level, data = new_records_model) |> as.data.frame()
exercise_dummies_new <- exercise_dummies_new[, !names(exercise_dummies_new) %in% "(Intercept)"]
new_records_model <- cbind(new_records_model[, !names(new_records_model) %in% "Exercise_Level"], exercise_dummies_new)

# Fixing names like in training process
names(new_records_model)[names(new_records_model) == "Phone_Usage_PurposeSocial Media"] <- "Phone_Usage_PurposeSocialMedia"
model_features <- setdiff(names(df_train_model), "Addiction_Level")
missing_cols <- setdiff(model_features, names(new_records_model))

for (col in missing_cols) {
  new_records_model[[col]] <- 0
}

new_records_model <- new_records_model[, model_features]

# Prediction - RF
new_records$Predicted_Addiction_Level <- predict(rf_model, newdata = new_records_model)

# Metrics on generated data
new_results <- postResample(pred = new_records$Predicted_Addiction_Level, obs = new_records$Addiction_Level)
print(new_results)
##     RMSE Rsquared      MAE 
## 5.656272 0.443224 5.569240
metrics_comparison <- rbind(Original_Test_Set = rf_results, Generated_Data = new_results)
print(metrics_comparison)
##                        RMSE  Rsquared       MAE
## Original_Test_Set 0.5270994 0.9016737 0.3713318
## Generated_Data    5.6562724 0.4432240 5.5692395

The genearted data consist of 500 new records. As we observed RF was great on the original datset, its performance is much worse on the synthetically generated dataset. This suggests that the generated observations are not fully in line with the relationships present in the original data. This simple script, which generates data in our experiment provided different distributions of the variables than in the original dataset. This led to reduced predictive power and shows that machine learning models generalize well only when new observations follow patterns similar to those present in the training data.
